questions.stem: Rearrange to form a correct sentence: 'morning/every/exercises/he/in/the'

options.option_text: He every morning exercises in the. (wrong: wrong word order)
He exercises every morning in the. (wrong: incomplete — 'in the' without noun)
He exercises in the morning every. (wrong: 'every' is at wrong position)
He exercises every morning. (correct: rearranges to 'He exercises every morning.' ✓ — 'in the' combines with morning)

questions.explanation: D is correct. Correct sentence: 'He exercises every morning.' Subject (He) + Verb (exercises) + Frequency adverb (every morning). The words 'in/the' combine with 'morning' but since 'every morning' is more natural here, the standard arrangement is: He exercises every morning.

questions.stem: Rearrange to form a correct sentence: 'spoke/he/clearly/very/English'

options.option_text: Very clearly he spoke English. (wrong: 'very clearly' should follow the verb+object)
He spoke English very clearly. (correct: Subject+Verb+Object+Adverb ✓)
He English spoke very clearly. (wrong: object 'English' must come after verb)
Clearly very English he spoke. (wrong: completely wrong order)

questions.explanation: B is correct. Correct sentence: 'He spoke English very clearly.' Pattern: Subject + Verb + Object + Adverb. 'He' (S) + 'spoke' (V) + 'English' (O) + 'very clearly' (Adverb of manner). Adverbs of manner typically come after the object.

questions.stem: Rearrange to form a correct sentence: 'have/books/how/you/many/read'?

options.option_text: How books many have you read? (wrong: 'many books' not 'books many')
How many books have you read? (correct: question order: How many + noun + auxiliary + subject + main verb ✓)
How many have you books read? (wrong: books should come right after 'many')
Have you read how many books? (wrong: question word 'how many' should come first)

questions.explanation: B is correct. Question word order: 'How many' + noun + auxiliary verb + subject + main verb. 'How MANY BOOKS have you READ?' This is a standard Wh-question structure with 'how many' as the question phrase.

options.option_text: Despite being ill, she finished her work on time. (correct: concessive clause + main clause ✓)
She finished her work on time despite being ill. (also correct: main clause + concessive clause; both orders acceptable)
She being ill despite finished her work on time. (wrong: wrong placement of 'being')
Despite she being ill, finished her work on time. (wrong: missing subject in main clause)

questions.explanation: A is correct. 'Despite being ill, she finished her work on time.' 'Despite + gerund phrase, Main clause.' Both option A and B are grammatically correct (comma version and no-comma version), but A (with the concessive clause first) is the canonical arrangement when 'despite' starts the sentence.

options.option_text: There was a great king once. (acceptable but less natural than 'there once was')
Once there was a great king. (correct: classic narrative opening; 'Once there was a great king' ✓)
A great king once was there. (wrong: 'was there' at end is awkward)
Great king once was there a. (wrong: article 'a' must precede noun)

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Once there was a great king.' Classic narrative/story-telling opening. Inverted word order: 'Once' (time adverb) + existential 'there was' + subject ('a great king'). Equally valid: 'There once was a great king.' Both are correct English.

options.option_text: You not should have chosen the third option. (wrong: 'not' misplaced)
You should not have chosen the third option. (correct: modal perfect negative ✓)
Should you not have chosen the third option? (wrong: this forms a question, not a statement)
You should have not chosen the third option. (wrong: 'not' should come before 'have', not between have and past participle)

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'You should NOT have chosen the third option.' Structure: Subject + Modal + NOT + have + V3 (past participle). In negative modal perfects, 'not' comes after the modal and before 'have.' 'Should have not' is non-standard; 'should not have' is correct.

options.option_text: I had hardly closed the door when the guests arrived. (correct: 'hardly...when' structure for two quick successive events ✓)
Hardly I had closed the door when the guests arrived. (wrong: subject-auxiliary inversion needed after 'hardly' at the start)
Hardly had I closed the door when the guests arrived. (also correct: inverted structure with 'hardly' at the start)
I closed the door hardly when guests the arrived. (wrong: word order jumbled)

questions.explanation: A is correct. 'I had hardly closed the door when the guests arrived.' This is the 'HARDLY...WHEN' construction for two events in quick succession. Both 'I had hardly' and 'Hardly had I' (inverted) are correct. Note: SCARCELY...WHEN and NO SOONER...THAN are similar constructions.

options.option_text: I was neither then able nor am I now. (wrong: awkward)
Neither was I able then, nor am I now. (correct: parallel neither...nor structure with inversion ✓)
Neither I was able then nor I am now. (wrong: no inversion in the neither/nor clauses)
I neither then was able, nor now am I. (wrong: unnatural word order)

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Neither was I able then, nor am I now.' When NEITHER or NOR begins a clause, subject-auxiliary inversion is required: 'Neither + auxiliary + subject + ...' and 'nor + auxiliary + subject + ...' This is a parallel structure with inversion for negative correlatives.

options.option_text: Never late than better. (wrong: this is a proverb; must be arranged correctly)
Late better than never. (wrong: order not correct for the proverb)
Better late than never. (correct: famous proverb meaning it's better to do something late than not at all ✓)
Never than better late. (wrong: reversed proverb)

questions.explanation: C is correct. 'BETTER LATE THAN NEVER.' This is the famous proverb meaning it's better to arrive/do something late than not to do it at all. Fixed expression. Note the comparative structure: 'Better X than Y' = X is preferable over Y.

options.option_text: He wisely invested money in to secure his future. (wrong: 'in to' should be 'to'; also awkward order)
He invested money wisely to secure his future. (correct: Subject+Verb+Object+Adverb+Infinitive purpose clause ✓)
Wisely he invested his future to secure money in. (wrong: garbled)
To secure his future, he invested money wisely. (also correct: purpose clause first, then main clause)

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'He invested money wisely to secure his future.' Structure: Subject + Verb + Object + Adverb + Infinitive clause (purpose). Both B and D are grammatically correct; B follows the standard declarative order with purpose at the end.
